doc.title: Gordon Lorraine — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Housewife years and growing political unrest
summary: Brown notes the shift to family life; Gordon says she was out of music and troubled by Vietnam and women's issues.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: So you have your kids, and you have a real shift in your lifestyle. It seems like instead of being a working woman, you were becoming more of a housewife, raising your two daughters, and then you got involved politically.
Oh yeah. In the peace movement.
Your daughters were born in the ‘50s, ‘50 and ‘52, I believe—Rebecca and Deborah.
Well, I was never even... Yeah, I was a housewife in a sense. I also had a job. I was always working. I was a working woman on the side.
But not involved in the music business.

No-no. No, I was not involved in the music business at all. However, the world was changing around me, and I was not a stupid woman, and I read a lot, and I was getting very unhappy about this war in Vietnam, and I was looking into women’s rights, and I was looking into a lot of things that were disturbing me as a thinking person who sees a lot of things wrong around her. The Vietnam War was a big issue. But I really got involved before the Vietnam War in the women’s peace issue...or was it the Vietnam War...
